scenarios.title: Building the Mithai Mahal Shop Page
scenarios.background: Mithai Mahal is a fictional family sweet shop in Varanasi that wants its first website, with a menu, photos and an 'Order on WhatsApp' button. A cousin built a draft: the order button is a div with a click handler, the three product cards have fixed pixel widths that overflow on phones, and every photo is a 4,000-pixel PNG straight from the camera. Most customers will visit on phones over mobile data.
constraints: Most visitors use phones on mobile data
The page must be usable with a keyboard and a screen reader
The shop has no budget for paid tools

questions.prompt: The 'Order on WhatsApp' control is a div with a click handler. Keyboard users cannot reach it, and screen readers do not announce it. What is the best fix?

options.text: Give the div a bright colour so the control stands out from the rest
Add a title attribute to the div that describes what the click does
Use a real link or button, which brings keyboard and reader support
Add a mouseover handler so the div reacts whenever it is hovered

questions.explanation: Native elements carry built-in behaviour: links and buttons can be focused with the Tab key, activated with Enter, and are announced with their role by screen readers. Since this control opens WhatsApp, a link to the WhatsApp URL is the natural element, and it gets all that for free.

why_others_wrong.a: Colour changes appearance only; the div still cannot be focused or announced.
why_others_wrong.b: A title attribute is unreliable for screen readers and does not make the div focusable.
why_others_wrong.d: Hover does not exist for keyboard and touch users, so it adds nothing for them.

questions.key_justification: Use semantic, native interactive elements instead of clickable divs.

questions.prompt: Three product cards sit side by side with fixed 400-pixel widths and overflow on phones. How should the layout be built?

options.text: Use CSS Grid with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)) for the cards
Put the cards in an HTML table with three columns and fixed widths
Position each card absolutely using exact pixel offsets from the top
Make a separate phone-only copy of the page with different HTML

questions.explanation: A grid with auto-fit and minmax fits as many cards per row as there is space for, each at least 250 pixels wide, and wraps them onto new rows on narrow screens. One fluid layout then works from small phones to wide desktops without overflow.

why_others_wrong.b: Tables are for tabular data, and fixed column widths overflow on phones in the same way.
why_others_wrong.c: Absolute positioning ignores screen size and breaks as soon as content or width changes.
why_others_wrong.d: A duplicate page doubles the maintenance and still has to guess which screen sizes count as phones.

questions.key_justification: Use fluid CSS Grid or Flexbox layouts that adapt to the available width.

questions.prompt: The camera photos make the page very slow on mobile data. Which two changes help most?

options.text: Serve resized images with srcset, in a modern format like WebP
Keep the 4,000-pixel PNGs and shrink them using CSS widths
Lazy-load the photos further down with loading="lazy"
Embed every photo as a base64 string inside the HTML file
Add more photos so that the page looks fuller while it loads

questions.explanation: Resized images in an efficient format, with srcset letting the browser pick a size that matches the screen, often cut each download by more than 90%. Lazy-loading photos that are below the visible area means they download only when the visitor scrolls near them.

why_others_wrong.b: CSS changes the display size but the full multi-megabyte file still downloads.
why_others_wrong.d: Base64 makes images about a third larger and stops the browser from caching them separately.
why_others_wrong.e: More photos add more data to download, which makes the page slower.

questions.key_justification: Send appropriately sized, compressed images and defer offscreen ones.

questions.prompt: Match each CSS feature to what it does.

targets.text: Sets which overlapping element is drawn on top
Counts padding and border inside the set width
Scales sizes with the root element's font size
Holds an element in place once you scroll to it

questions.explanation: With border-box, a 300-pixel-wide box stays 300 pixels however much padding it has. Sticky positioning scrolls an element normally until it reaches an edge and then holds it there, z-index orders overlapping positioned elements, and rem units scale with the root font size, so they respect a user's text-size setting.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Confusing sticky with fixed positioning: a fixed element is always pinned to the screen, while a sticky one scrolls with the page until it reaches its set edge.

questions.key_justification: These properties control box sizing, scroll behaviour, stacking and scalable units.

scenarios.title: Getting State Right in the Yatra Kosh Search App
scenarios.background: Yatra Kosh is a fictional travel site in Jaipur, built as a React single-page app, where people search buses and trains and book tickets. The search box calls the API on every keystroke, users lose their filters when they refresh or share a link, deleting a passenger row in the booking form sometimes shows the wrong names in the remaining rows, and data passes through six layers of components. The team must fix these before the holiday rush.
constraints: The search API is rate-limited to protect the backend
Search links are often shared on WhatsApp
The front end is React; the API is maintained by another team

questions.prompt: Typing 'Jodhpur' in the search box fires seven API requests, one per letter, and hits the rate limit. What should change?

options.text: Debounce the input and search once typing has paused for ~300 ms
Ask the API team to remove the rate limit for the search endpoint
Send each keystroke's request but hide every result except the last
Load the full timetable for every route when the app first opens

questions.explanation: Debouncing waits until the user pauses typing before sending a request, so a burst of keystrokes becomes one search. Cancelling any in-flight request when a new one starts, for example with an AbortController, saves even more work.

why_others_wrong.b: The limit protects the backend; removing it shifts the overload onto the API team.
why_others_wrong.c: Every request is still sent, so the rate limit is hit just the same.
why_others_wrong.d: A full timetable is a huge download for each visitor and is quickly out of date.

questions.key_justification: Debounce rapid input so that requests fire only after the user pauses.

questions.prompt: Users lose their filters on refresh, and links shared on WhatsApp open an empty search. Where should the filter state live?

options.text: In component state only, which resets when the page is reloaded
In the URL's query parameters, read when the page first loads
In a cookie that the server reads only when users are logged in
In a global variable on the window object, set when filters change

questions.explanation: Putting search filters in the URL, such as ?from=JP&to=JU&date=2026-11-02, means a refresh restores them, the back button works, and a shared link opens the same search for the person who receives it.

why_others_wrong.a: Component state lives only in memory, so a refresh or a shared link loses it.
why_others_wrong.c: A cookie stays on the sender's browser, so the person who receives a shared link sees none of it.
why_others_wrong.d: A window variable is lost on refresh just like component state.

questions.key_justification: Shareable, refresh-safe view state belongs in the URL.

questions.prompt: The passenger list uses each row's array index as its React key. After deleting the second row, the third row shows the deleted passenger's name in its input. Why, and what is the fix?

options.text: React is buggy with forms; replace every input with plain text
The names are too long; trim them before they are put in state
Index keys shift on delete; key each row by a stable unique id
The list needs a re-render; reload the page after each delete

questions.explanation: React uses keys to match rows between renders. When a row is deleted, every later row's index shifts, so React reuses the wrong row's input state for the remaining passengers. Giving each passenger a stable unique id as its key keeps state attached to the right row.

why_others_wrong.a: React handles forms reliably when keys are stable; the bug is in the key choice.
why_others_wrong.b: Name length has nothing to do with which row's state is reused.
why_others_wrong.d: Reloading loses the whole form, which is far worse than the bug.

questions.key_justification: Use stable, unique keys for list items, never array indexes when items can move.

questions.prompt: The booking form collects passenger names and ages. Which two validation practices are correct?

options.text: Validate in the browser so mistakes are shown as soon as possible
Rely on the browser checks alone, since users cannot get past them
Validate again on the server, because browser checks can be skipped
Allow only English letters A to Z in passenger name fields
Validate on the server only and show no messages in the browser

questions.explanation: Checks in the browser give instant, friendly feedback, such as 'Age must be a number'. They can be bypassed by anyone sending requests directly, so the server must validate everything again before booking.

why_others_wrong.b: Browser checks are easily bypassed with developer tools or direct API calls.
why_others_wrong.d: Many passengers' names contain other scripts, spaces or punctuation, so this rejects valid names.
why_others_wrong.e: Users then find mistakes only after submitting, which is slower and more frustrating.

questions.key_justification: Validate on the client for experience and on the server for correctness.

questions.prompt: Match each front-end problem to the technique that fixes it.

items.text: An older search's results arrive late and overwrite the newer ones
The user's currency is passed down through six component layers
A 5,000-row results list re-renders slowly as the user scrolls
Four components each fetch the same station list separately

targets.text: Render only the visible rows with a virtualised list
Use a shared data-fetching cache keyed by the request
Cancel or ignore responses that are not for the latest request
Provide the value through React context or a state store

questions.explanation: Out-of-order responses are a race, fixed by cancelling stale requests or ignoring responses that do not match the latest query. Values needed deep in the tree come from context or a store instead of being passed through every layer, long lists render only the visible rows, and repeated fetches share one cached request.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Fixing the out-of-order results with a debounce: debouncing reduces how many requests are sent, but two requests can still finish in the wrong order.

questions.key_justification: Races, deep props, long lists and repeated fetches each have a standard fix.

code_pool.prompt: Yatra Kosh's search box called the API on every keystroke. With debouncing, each keystroke restarts a timer and the search runs only when the user pauses. The first line is `delay n`, the second has n keystroke times in milliseconds, in order. Complete `debounce`: each keystroke starts a fresh timer of `delay` ms that replaces the previous one; a call fires when a timer runs out, and a keystroke at or after that moment does not cancel it. The program prints `calls k` and `at` with the firing times, or `at -`.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def debounce(keys, delay):
    """keys: keystroke times in ms, in order. Each keystroke (re)starts a timer of `delay` ms; the search call fires when a timer runs out. A keystroke at or after the moment a timer runs out does not cancel it. Return the times the call fires."""
    # Write your code here.
    return [t + delay for t in keys]


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    delay, n = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
    keys = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
    calls = debounce(keys, delay)
    print("calls", len(calls))
    print("at", " ".join(map(str, calls)) if calls else "-")


main()
code_pool.reference_solution:
import sys


def debounce(keys, delay):
    """keys: keystroke times in ms, in order. Each keystroke (re)starts a timer of `delay` ms; the search call fires when a timer runs out. A keystroke at or after the moment a timer runs out does not cancel it. Return the times the call fires."""
    calls = []
    for i, t in enumerate(keys):
        is_last = i == len(keys) - 1
        if is_last or keys[i + 1] >= t + delay:     # nobody typed before this timer ran out
            calls.append(t + delay)
    return calls


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    delay, n = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
    keys = list(map(int, data[2:2 + n]))
    calls = debounce(keys, delay)
    print("calls", len(calls))
    print("at", " ".join(map(str, calls)) if calls else "-")


main()
code_pool.explanation: A keystroke's timer survives only if the next keystroke comes at or after it expires, so one look at the next time decides each one. Debouncing turns a burst of typing into one request, cutting load on the API and avoiding out-of-order results for half-typed queries.
code_pool.key_justification: Debounce as a scan comparing each event with the next.

code_pool.prompt: Users lose their filters when they refresh or share a link, so the search state moves into the URL. Write the reading side. The input is one URL or query string. Complete `parse_query`: take the part after the first `?` (or the whole line if there is none), split on `&` and skip empty pieces; each piece is `key=value` (no `=` means an empty value); decode `+` as a space and `%XX` as the character with that hex code. A key can repeat (class=sleeper&class=3A). The program prints `key=v1,v2` per key, sorted by key, values in the order they appeared, or EMPTY.
code_pool.explanation: Splitting on '&' and then on the first '=' gives key-value pairs; a dictionary of lists keeps repeated keys (multi-select filters) in order. Decoding must happen after splitting, so an encoded '&' (%26) inside a value is not mistaken for a separator. URLSearchParams does the same in the browser.
code_pool.key_justification: Tokenise and percent-decode a query string into a multi-map.

scenarios.title: Slow and Jumpy Pages at Pustak Ghar
scenarios.background: Pustak Ghar is a fictional online bookshop in Kozhikode. Its book pages score badly on Core Web Vitals: the content jumps when images and ad slots load, the large hero image appears late because it is added by JavaScript after a big bundle runs, and the browser blocks requests from the shop at shop.pustakghar.in to the API at api.pustakghar.in with a CORS error. Staff also say the admin app gets slower the longer it stays open.
constraints: Search ranking and conversions depend on Core Web Vitals
The shop and the API run on different subdomains
Staff keep the admin single-page app open all day

questions.prompt: Text jumps down the page as book covers and an ad slot load, and readers tap the wrong links. What fixes this layout shift?

options.text: Load the covers and the ad last, after the rest of the page
Hide the whole page until every single image has loaded
Set width, height or aspect-ratio and reserve space for the ad
Add a CSS fade-in animation to each image as it finishes loading

questions.explanation: Content shifts when the browser does not know how much space an image or ad will take until it arrives. Giving images width and height attributes or a CSS aspect-ratio, and giving the ad slot a fixed minimum size, reserves the space up front, so nothing moves when they load.

why_others_wrong.a: Loading them later still pushes content down when they appear, possibly while the reader is reading.
why_others_wrong.b: Hiding the page delays everything and hurts loading metrics badly.
why_others_wrong.d: A fade-in changes how images appear, not the space they suddenly take up.

questions.key_justification: Prevent layout shift by reserving space for media and dynamic content.

questions.prompt: The hero image is the page's largest element, but it is added by JavaScript after a 900 KB bundle runs, so it appears late. What helps most?

options.text: Add the image in an even later script, after analytics has run
Put the image in the HTML with high fetch priority, compressed
Load the image with loading="lazy" so it downloads only on scroll
Turn the image into a CSS background that the bundle sets later

questions.explanation: Largest Contentful Paint measures when the biggest visible element appears. Placing the hero image directly in the HTML lets the browser find and fetch it immediately, and fetchpriority="high" plus a compressed modern format makes it arrive sooner, instead of waiting for the bundle.

why_others_wrong.a: Delaying the image further makes the largest element appear even later.
why_others_wrong.c: Lazy-loading the visible hero image delays the very element that is being measured.
why_others_wrong.d: A background set by the bundle is still discovered only after the script runs.

questions.key_justification: Make the largest above-the-fold element discoverable early and prioritised.

questions.prompt: The browser blocks fetch calls from shop.pustakghar.in to api.pustakghar.in with a CORS error. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Ask customers to install a browser extension that disables CORS
Set mode: 'no-cors' on every fetch call made by the shop page
Wrap the fetch in try-catch and quietly ignore the CORS errors
Have the API allow the shop's origin with CORS response headers

questions.explanation: Browsers block cross-origin reads unless the server says they are allowed. The API must answer with Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to https://shop.pustakghar.in, and handle preflight requests for methods and headers it accepts, so the browser lets the shop read the responses.

why_others_wrong.a: Customers will not install extensions, and turning off browser security is dangerous.
why_others_wrong.b: no-cors makes the response unreadable to the page, so the shop still gets no data.
why_others_wrong.c: Ignoring the error does not deliver the data the page needs.

questions.key_justification: CORS is fixed on the server by allowing the trusted origin.

questions.prompt: The admin app gets slower the longer it stays open. Which two causes are most likely?

options.text: Event listeners added each time a view mounts and never removed
The CSS file is a little larger than it was at the last release
Timers started with setInterval that are not cleared on unmount
HTML comments that are left in the page's markup by developers
The app's favicon is a PNG image rather than an SVG image

questions.explanation: A slowdown that grows with time points to something accumulating. Listeners added on every mount without cleanup, and intervals that keep running after their view is gone, pile up work and memory each time staff navigate around the app.

why_others_wrong.b: A slightly larger CSS file loads once; it does not grow worse over time.
why_others_wrong.d: Comments are parsed once and cost almost nothing.
why_others_wrong.e: The favicon's format has no effect on runtime speed.

questions.key_justification: Gradual slowdowns come from uncleaned listeners, timers and references.

code_pool.prompt: The shop at https://shop.pustakghar.in calls an API on another origin, and the browser blocks it unless the API allows that origin. Check the API's CORS settings against real requests. The first line lists the allowed origins (exactly scheme://host[:port], or `*` for any), the second the allowed methods, the third is n, then n requests `origin method`. Complete `cors_allows`: a request is allowed only if the origin matches exactly (http and https, and different ports, are different origins) or `*` is listed, and the method is allowed. The program prints `origin method ALLOW|BLOCK` per request, then `blocked k`.

import sys


def cors_allows(origins, methods, origin, method):
    """origins: allowed origins exactly as scheme://host[:port], or '*' for any. methods: allowed methods. Return True if this cross-origin request is allowed: the origin matches exactly (or '*' is listed) and the method is allowed."""
    # Write your code here.
    return True


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    origins = data[0].split()
    methods = data[1].split()
    n = int(data[2])
    blocked = 0
    for i in range(n):
        origin, method = data[3 + i].split()
        ok = cors_allows(origins, methods, origin, method)
        blocked += not ok
        print(origin, method, "ALLOW" if ok else "BLOCK")
    print("blocked", blocked)


main()
code_pool.reference_solution:
import sys


def cors_allows(origins, methods, origin, method):
    """origins: allowed origins exactly as scheme://host[:port], or '*' for any. methods: allowed methods. Return True if this cross-origin request is allowed: the origin matches exactly (or '*' is listed) and the method is allowed."""
    allowed_origins, allowed_methods = set(origins), set(methods)
    origin_ok = "*" in allowed_origins or origin in allowed_origins     # exact match: scheme, host and port
    return origin_ok and method in allowed_methods


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    origins = data[0].split()
    methods = data[1].split()
    n = int(data[2])
    blocked = 0
    for i in range(n):
        origin, method = data[3 + i].split()
        ok = cors_allows(origins, methods, origin, method)
        blocked += not ok
        print(origin, method, "ALLOW" if ok else "BLOCK")
    print("blocked", blocked)


main()
code_pool.explanation: An origin is the exact triple of scheme, host and port, so set membership on the full string is the right test; 'shop.pustakghar.in' over http is a different origin from https. The fix belongs on the API, which must list the shop's origin; nothing in the front end can make the browser skip this check.
code_pool.key_justification: Exact-match set look-ups for an origin and method allow-list.

import sys


def cls(shifts):
    """shifts: (time ms, score in ten-thousandths, had_recent_input 0/1) in time order. Ignore shifts right after user input. Group the rest into session windows: a shift starts a new window if it comes more than 1000 ms after the previous counted shift, or more than 5000 ms after the window's first shift. Return (the largest window sum, number of windows)."""
    best = windows = 0
    start = last = None
    total = 0
    for t, score, had_input in shifts:
        if had_input:
            continue                                  # expected shifts after a click do not count
        if start is None or t - last > 1000 or t - start > 5000:
            windows += 1
            start, total = t, 0
        total += score
        last = t
        best = max(best, total)
    return best, windows


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    shifts = [tuple(map(int, data[1 + i].split())) for i in range(n)]
    best, windows = cls(shifts)
    print("cls", f"{best / 10000:.4f}")
    print("windows", windows)


main()
code_pool.explanation: One pass with the current window's start, last time and sum is enough: a gap over a second or a window older than five seconds starts a new one, and CLS keeps the worst window, not the total. Reserving space for images and ad slots (width and height, aspect-ratio) is what actually removes these shifts.
code_pool.key_justification: Session windows over a time-ordered array (CLS definition).

scenarios.title: Keeping the Dhanda Dost Dashboard Fast and Maintainable
scenarios.background: Dhanda Dost is a fictional accounting web app for small shops in Coimbatore. Its JavaScript bundle has grown to 3 MB, mostly because a charting library loads even on the login page. Four front-end developers are debating whether to build their own component library, how to test a growing app that breaks often, and what to do about the 15% of users on old Android phones with outdated browsers.
constraints: Shop owners log in on low-cost phones over mobile data
Four front-end developers support the whole app
Old Android browsers lack some modern JavaScript features

questions.prompt: The 3 MB bundle includes the charting library even on the login page. What is the best fix?

options.text: Minify the bundle once more and keep shipping it as a single file
Split code by route and load the charts only on the reports pages
Remove every chart from the app to make the bundle a lot smaller
Ask users to keep the app open all day so it rarely needs to load

questions.explanation: Route-based code splitting with dynamic import() loads each page's code only when it is visited. The login page then downloads a small bundle, and the charting library arrives only when a user opens a report.

why_others_wrong.a: The bundle is presumably already minified, so another pass saves little while every page still loads everything.
why_others_wrong.c: Charts are a core feature of an accounting dashboard.
why_others_wrong.d: Users cannot avoid first loads, and the login page is always loaded first.

questions.key_justification: Split bundles by route so each page loads only the code it needs.

questions.prompt: Should the four developers build their own component library from scratch?

options.text: Yes, because a custom library is always faster than any other
Yes, and they should also build their own date and number logic
No; avoid shared components and write each screen's widgets fresh
No; theme a mature, accessible open-source library to match the brand

questions.explanation: Accessible dropdowns, dialogs and date pickers take a lot of work to get right. A small team gets more value from a well-tested open-source component library themed to its brand, and can spend its time on the accounting features customers pay for.

why_others_wrong.a: Custom components are not inherently faster, and building them costs months of a small team's time.
why_others_wrong.b: Rebuilding date and number handling adds even more risk for no user benefit.
why_others_wrong.c: Writing widgets afresh on every screen creates inconsistent, duplicated and buggy code.

questions.key_justification: Small teams should adopt and theme proven components rather than build them from scratch.

questions.prompt: The app keeps breaking in production. Which testing strategy should the team adopt?

options.text: Only end-to-end browser tests, covering every screen in the app
Many unit tests, component tests that act like users, few E2E
Manual testing by the developers just before each release only
Snapshot tests of every component's HTML and nothing besides

questions.explanation: Fast unit tests cover logic such as tax calculations, component tests check behaviour the way a user interacts, with tools like Testing Library, and a small set of end-to-end tests covers critical journeys such as creating an invoice. This mix gives broad coverage that runs quickly and fails for meaningful reasons.

why_others_wrong.a: Testing everything end to end is slow and flaky, so developers stop trusting and running the tests.
why_others_wrong.c: Manual checks before release miss regressions and do not scale as the app grows.
why_others_wrong.d: Snapshots catch markup changes, not broken behaviour, and are often updated without review.

questions.key_justification: Balance many fast unit and component tests with a few end-to-end tests of critical flows.

questions.prompt: 15% of users are on old Android browsers that lack some modern features. Which two approaches fit best?

options.text: Make core tasks work without the newest browser features
Block old browsers and show an 'upgrade your phone' page
Transpile and polyfill based on a target browser list
Send every polyfill that exists to every user's browser
Ignore old browsers, since they are only a small group

questions.explanation: Progressive enhancement keeps core tasks such as recording a sale working on older browsers while adding extras where they are supported. A target browser list tells the build tools exactly which syntax to transpile and which features to polyfill, so older browsers work without bloating the code for everyone else.

why_others_wrong.b: Blocking 15% of paying shop owners loses customers who cannot easily buy a new phone.
why_others_wrong.d: Shipping every polyfill makes the app heavier for everyone, including modern browsers.
why_others_wrong.e: Fifteen percent is a large share of customers to leave with a broken app.

questions.key_justification: Support older browsers with progressive enhancement and targeted transpiling and polyfills.

import sys


def tenths(text):
    whole, _, frac = text.partition(".")
    return int(whole) * 10 + int((frac + "0")[:1])


def cover(rows, target):
    """rows: (browser, version, share %) with shares like '12.5'. target: percent like '90'. Take browsers by share, largest first (ties by browser then version), until the total reaches the target. Return (the chosen (browser, version), total share in tenths of a percent)."""
    goal = tenths(target)
    ranked = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (-tenths(r[2]), r[0], r[1]))
    chosen, total = [], 0
    for browser, version, share in ranked:
        if total >= goal:
            break
        chosen.append((browser, version))
        total += tenths(share)
    return chosen, total


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    target = data[0].strip()
    n = int(data[1])
    rows = [tuple(data[2 + i].split()) for i in range(n)]
    chosen, covered = cover(rows, target)
    for name, version in chosen:
        print(name, version)
    print("browsers", len(chosen))
    print("covered", f"{covered // 10}.{covered % 10}%")


main()
code_pool.explanation: Sorting by share and taking from the top until the target is reached gives the smallest set that covers it (the greedy choice is optimal here because each browser only adds share). Doing the sums in tenths keeps 90.0 from turning into 89.99999. It turns a debate into a support policy anyone can recheck when the analytics change.
code_pool.key_justification: Sort by share, then a cumulative cut-off.

scenarios.title: Launching the Sangam Tickets Flash Sale
scenarios.background: Sangam Tickets is a fictional ticketing site in Bengaluru. For a big concert, 100,000 fans will arrive the minute sales open to pick seats on an interactive seat map. The front-end team is building the seat map and checkout. It must stay fast on mid-range phones, show seats being taken in near real time, work with keyboards and screen readers, and support English, Kannada and Tamil. Last year the site's front end fell over in the first minute.
constraints: 100,000 visitors arrive within the first minute
The site must be accessible and available in three languages

questions.prompt: Put the steps for shipping the new seat map in order.

options.text: Deploy a preview build for QA and design review
Build the components from the shared design tokens
Release to production while watching real-user metrics
Write component and integration tests for the seat map
Run automated performance and accessibility checks in CI

questions.explanation: The seat map is built from shared tokens and covered by tests, and CI then checks performance and accessibility automatically on every change. A preview deployment lets QA and designers review the real build, and the release goes out with real-user monitoring watching how it behaves.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Sending the build for QA review before the automated checks run, which spends people's time on problems a machine would have caught in minutes.

questions.key_justification: Build, test, check automatically, review a preview, then release with monitoring.

questions.prompt: 100,000 fans will load the site in the same minute. How should the front end's static files be served?

options.text: From the main app server, with caching turned off to stay fresh
Via a CDN, with hashed filenames and long cache times
From one server in Mumbai that is upgraded for the sale day
As one huge HTML file with all scripts and styles inlined

questions.explanation: A CDN serves files from servers close to each fan and absorbs the spike. Content-hashed filenames, such as app.3f9a1c.js, can be cached for a year because every new build gets new names, while the small HTML page is cached briefly so it always points to the latest files.

why_others_wrong.a: Serving every file from the app server without caching overloads it in the first seconds.
why_others_wrong.c: One server, however large, is a single bottleneck and is far from many fans.
why_others_wrong.d: Inlining everything prevents caching and makes every page load download the whole site.

questions.key_justification: Serve static assets from a CDN with cache-busting filenames and long cache lifetimes.

questions.prompt: Last year, fans saw blank screens, but the team only heard about it on social media. What should be in place this year?

options.text: Ask fans to email screenshots whenever they run into a problem
Rely on the developers' own laptops showing no console errors
Track JS errors with source maps, plus real-user monitoring
Check the server's CPU graph in the hours after the sale ends

questions.explanation: An error-tracking service records JavaScript errors from real visitors, and source maps turn them back into readable code locations. Real-user monitoring of load times and Core Web Vitals shows slowdowns as they happen, so the team learns about problems in seconds rather than from social media.

why_others_wrong.a: Few fans email, and screenshots arrive far too late during a one-minute rush.
why_others_wrong.b: Developers' laptops and networks are nothing like fans' phones.
why_others_wrong.d: Server CPU says nothing about JavaScript errors in fans' browsers, and checking afterwards is too late.

questions.key_justification: Monitor real users' errors and performance in production.

questions.prompt: Which two choices make the seat map accessible?

options.text: Make seats keyboard-reachable with arrow keys and a visible focus
Show seat details only in tooltips that appear on mouse hover
Give each seat a name like 'Row F, seat 12, available, 1,500 rupees'
Mark available and sold seats by colour alone to keep it simple
Disable pinch-to-zoom so the map always stays at a single size

questions.explanation: Keyboard navigation with a clear focus indicator lets people who cannot use a mouse or touch screen pick seats. A descriptive accessible name for each seat tells screen-reader users its row, number, status and price.

why_others_wrong.b: Hover does not exist for keyboard, touch or screen-reader users.
why_others_wrong.d: Colour alone fails for colour-blind users and says nothing to screen readers.
why_others_wrong.e: Blocking zoom stops low-vision users from enlarging the small seats.

questions.key_justification: Interactive widgets need keyboard operation and meaningful accessible names.

questions.prompt: Match each requirement to the technique that delivers it.

items.text: Seats taken by others should disappear within a second
The site must stay usable on a slow 3G connection
Prices and dates appear in English, Kannada and Tamil
A crash in the seat map must not blank the whole page

targets.text: An error boundary around the seat map component
Live updates over WebSocket or server-sent events
Translation files and locale-aware Intl formatting
A performance budget that limits JavaScript size

questions.explanation: Pushing seat changes over a WebSocket or server-sent events updates the map almost instantly. A performance budget keeps the code light enough for slow connections, translation files with Intl formatting show text, prices and dates correctly for each language, and an error boundary contains a crash so the rest of the page keeps working.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Polling the server every second for seat changes: with 100,000 fans this creates a flood of requests, while a pushed stream sends only the changes.

questions.key_justification: Real-time pushes, budgets, internationalisation and error boundaries each meet a launch need.

import re
import sys


def cache_header(name):
    """Return the Cache-Control value for a file: .html files get 'no-cache'; files whose name has a content hash, a part of exactly 8 lowercase hex characters between dots before the extension (app.3f9a1c2b.js), get 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable'; everything else gets 'public, max-age=3600'."""
    if name.endswith(".html"):
        return "no-cache"
    base = name.rsplit("/", 1)[-1]
    if re.search(r"\.[0-9a-f]{8}\.", base):          # .3f9a1c2b. : the content changes the name
        return "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"
    return "public, max-age=3600"


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    for i in range(n):
        name = data[1 + i].strip()
        print(name, cache_header(name))


main()

The HTML that references those names must not be cached long, or users keep loading the old release. Everything else gets a short, safe lifetime. The rule is a small pattern match on the file name.
code_pool.key_justification: Classify file names with a pattern to choose cache headers.

The first line is the hold time in seconds, the second is n, then n events `second action seat user` in time order (action HOLD, RELEASE or BUY). Complete `run_sale`: a hold expires at second >= start + hold time. HOLD works if the seat is not sold and nobody else holds it (holding your own seat again restarts the timer); RELEASE works only for the current holder; BUY works only for the current holder of an unexpired hold and sells the seat. import sys


def run_sale(events, hold):
    """events: (second, HOLD|RELEASE|BUY, seat, user) in time order. A hold lasts `hold` seconds (it has expired at second >= start + hold). HOLD works if the seat is not sold and nobody else holds it (holding your own seat again restarts the timer). RELEASE works only for the current holder. BUY works only for the current holder of an unexpired hold, and sells the seat. Anything else is rejected. Return ([(seat, buyer)] sorted by seat, number of rejected events)."""
    # Write your code here.
    return [], 0


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    hold = int(data[0])
    n = int(data[1])
    events = []
    for i in range(n):
        t, action, seat, user = data[2 + i].split()
        events.append((int(t), action, seat, user))
    sold, rejected = run_sale(events, hold)
    for seat, user in sold:
        print(seat, user)
    print("rejected", rejected)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Per-seat dictionaries for the holder, the expiry time and the buyer make every event an O(1) check. Treating an expired hold as absent, rather than running a cleanup job, means a seat frees itself at exactly the right second. The server must enforce this; the seat map in the browser only displays it.
